systemdesign-framework.tldr:
• Spend 45 minutes as: requirements, estimation, API and data model, high-level design, deep dives, wrap-up.
  • Ask about users, read/write ratio, latency, consistency and must-have features first.
  • Justify every component with a requirement and state what you give up.
  • Narrate; don't jump to boxes or over-design for imaginary scale.
systemdesign-framework.body:
The interviewer is grading how you think, not whether you reach a "correct" diagram. They look for: clarifying ambiguity, reasonable scoping, numbers that drive decisions, a clean high-level design, depth in one or two areas, and honest trade-offs.

The timeline

Minutes Step What to produce
0–5 Requirements functional (3–5 core features), non-functional (scale, latency, availability, consistency), out of scope
5–10 Estimation QPS (read and write), storage over 5 years, bandwidth, cache size — only what changes decisions
10–15 API + data model 3–5 endpoints; main entities, keys and access patterns
15–25 High-level design client → LB/gateway → services → storage/cache/queue; walk one request end to end
25–40 Deep dives the 1–2 hardest parts (the interviewer often picks): scaling the hot path, consistency, failure handling
40–45 Wrap-up bottlenecks, monitoring, what you'd do with more time

Questions to ask at the start

  • Who are the users and how many? DAU, peak multiplier, geography.
  • Read-heavy or write-heavy? What's the read:write ratio?
  • What latency is acceptable for the core path? (e.g. p99 under 200 ms)
  • Consistency: can users see stale data for a few seconds? Is losing data ever acceptable?
  • Must-have features vs nice-to-have. Mobile, web, or both?

Non-functional requirements checklist: scalability, availability (99.9% = 8.7 h downtime/year; 99.99% = 52 min), latency, consistency model, durability, security/privacy, cost.

Interview tip narrate trade-offs as "I'm choosing X because of requirement Y; the cost is Z." Saying what you are giving up is what separates SDE2 answers from SDE1 answers.

Common mistakes: jumping to boxes before requirements; spending 15 minutes on estimation; naming technologies without justifying them ("use Kafka" — why?); designing for Google scale when the problem says 10k users; ignoring failure modes; going silent while thinking.

The reference architecture most designs start from

Say it in one breath, then spend your time on what's specific to the problem: the data model, the hot path and the hard trade-off.

Standard building blocks to reach for

Need Building block
Spread traffic, health checks Load balancer (L4/L7)
Single entry, auth, rate limits API gateway
Reduce read latency / DB load Cache (Redis), CDN for static/media
Decouple, absorb spikes, fan-out Message queue / log (Kafka, SQS)
Relational data, transactions PostgreSQL / MySQL (+ read replicas, sharding)
Huge write volume, simple key access Cassandra / DynamoDB
Full-text search Elasticsearch / OpenSearch
Files, images, video Object storage (S3) + CDN
Unique IDs Snowflake / UUIDv7 / DB sequences with ranges
Coordination, leader election ZooKeeper / etcd
Analytics data lake + batch/stream processing (Spark, Flink)

systemdesign-estimation.tldr:
• 1M requests/day ≈ 12 QPS; a day ≈ 10⁵ seconds; peaks are 2–3× (10× for events).
  • Estimate QPS, storage over years, bandwidth and cache size only where they change decisions.
  • Say assumptions out loud and draw the conclusion immediately.
  • Memorize rough capacities: Redis ~100k ops/s, a DB ~5–10k writes/s, an app server ~1–5k req/s.
systemdesign-estimation.body:
Estimation exists to make decisions: one DB or sharded? Does the hot set fit in memory? How many servers? Round aggressively.

Numbers to memorize

Quantity Value
Seconds per day ~86,400 ≈ 10⁵
1 million requests/day ≈ 12 QPS
100 million requests/day ≈ 1,200 QPS
1 billion requests/day ≈ 12,000 QPS
Peak traffic 2–3× average (10× for events/sales)
char / int / long / UUID 1 B / 4 B / 8 B / 16 B
Typical metadata row 100 B – 1 KB
Image (compressed) 200 KB – 2 MB
1 minute of 720p video ~50 MB
Single Redis node ~100k ops/s
Single well-tuned Postgres/MySQL ~5–10k simple writes/s, more reads
Single app server (Spring Boot, simple endpoint) ~1–5k req/s
Kafka partition ~10 MB/s comfortably

Powers of two: 2¹⁰ ≈ 1 thousand (KB), 2²⁰ ≈ 1 million (MB), 2³⁰ ≈ 1 billion (GB), 2⁴⁰ ≈ 1 trillion (TB).

Worked example — a photo-sharing app

Text
Users:        100M DAU, each views 50 photos and uploads 0.1 photo per day
Reads:        100M × 50 / 10^5 s     = 50,000 QPS  (peak ~150k)
Writes:       100M × 0.1 / 10^5 s    = 100 uploads/s
Read:write    500:1  -> read-heavy: CDN + cache are the core of the design
Storage/day:  10M photos × 1 MB      = 10 TB/day -> ~3.6 PB/year -> object storage, not a DB
Metadata:     10M rows/day × 500 B   = 5 GB/day -> ~2 TB/year -> fits a sharded SQL or Cassandra
Cache:        20% of daily-read metadata is hot -> tens of GB -> a small Redis cluster

Interview tip state assumptions out loud, write the math on the board, and immediately draw the conclusion ("so writes are trivial; reads dominate; I'll focus on caching").

From QPS to servers — a second worked example

Text
Peak read QPS:              150,000
Cache hit ratio:            95%   -> 7,500 QPS reach the database
One app instance:           ~2,000 req/s for a cached JSON endpoint -> 75 instances at peak, ~100 with headroom
Redis:                      150k ops/s -> 2-3 primaries (shard for headroom, not capacity)
DB reads after cache:       7,500 QPS -> primary + 2-3 read replicas
Bandwidth (egress):         150k × 5 KB = 750 MB/s ≈ 6 Gbps -> CDN for anything cacheable

Availability math: components in series multiply (0.999 × 0.999 = 0.998); redundant components in parallel fail only together (1 − (0.01 × 0.01) = 0.9999 for two 99% replicas). This is why every tier gets at least two instances across availability zones.

Availability Downtime / year Downtime / month
99% 3.65 days 7.3 h
99.9% 8.8 h 44 min
99.95% 4.4 h 22 min
99.99% 53 min 4.4 min
99.999% 5.3 min 26 s

systemdesign-urlshortener.tldr:
• Generate codes with range-allocated counters + base62 (or pre-generated keys); scramble to avoid guessable ids.
  • Redirects are the hot path: cache in Redis, 302 to keep analytics accurate.
  • Send click analytics asynchronously through Kafka.
  • Handle aliases, expiry and abuse with unique constraints, TTLs and rate limits.
systemdesign-urlshortener.body:
Requirements

  • Functional: create a short URL for a long URL (optional custom alias, optional expiry); redirect short → long; basic click analytics.
  • Non-functional: redirects are the hot path (low latency, very high availability); short codes are unique and not guessable in sequence; read-heavy (100:1).

Estimation

Text
New URLs:   100M/month ≈ 40 writes/s
Redirects:  100:1 -> ~4,000 QPS average, ~10k peak
Storage:    100M/month × 12 months × 5 years × 500 B ≈ 3 TB
Code space: base62, 7 chars = 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion -> plenty

API

Text
POST /api/v1/urls          { "longUrl": "...", "alias": "optional", "expiresAt": "optional" }
                           -> 201 { "shortUrl": "https://sho.rt/aB3x9Kq" }
GET  /{code}               -> 302 Location: <longUrl>     (or 301; see trade-off below)
GET  /api/v1/urls/{code}/stats

Data model: urls(code PK, long_url, user_id, created_at, expires_at). Simple key-value access → DynamoDB/Cassandra, or a sharded MySQL keyed by code.

Generating short codes — the core deep dive

Approach How Pros Cons
Hash + truncate MD5/SHA of URL, first 7 base62 chars stateless, same URL → same code collisions need check-and-retry
Counter + base62 global counter encoded in base62 no collisions, short central counter is a bottleneck; codes are predictable
Range allocation each server leases a block of 1M ids from ZooKeeper/DB, encodes locally no per-request coordination lost ranges on crash (harmless)
Pre-generated keys offline service fills a table of unused codes fast, random-looking extra service and table
Java
public final class Base62 {
    private static final char[] ALPHABET =
        "0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ".toCharArray();

    public static String encode(long id) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        do { sb.append(ALPHABET[(int) (id % 62)]); id /= 62; } while (id > 0);
        return sb.reverse().toString();
    }
}

// Range allocation: each instance leases ids in blocks
@Component
public class IdRangeAllocator {
    private final RangeRepository ranges;     // UPDATE counters SET next = next + :block ... RETURNING
    private long next, end;
    public synchronized long nextId() {
        if (next >= end) { long start = ranges.leaseBlock(1_000_000); next = start; end = start + 1_000_000; }
        return next++;
    }
}
// To avoid sequential, guessable codes: run the id through a bijective scramble
// (e.g. multiply by a large odd constant mod 62^7, or a Feistel cipher) before base62.

Redirect path: cache-aside in Redis (code → longUrl), TTL a few hours; 80/20 popularity means a modest cache absorbs most reads. Cache misses for unknown codes (scanners) → cache negative results or a Bloom filter.

Create path with a leased id range

301 vs 302: 301 (permanent) lets browsers cache, reducing load but losing analytics after the first visit. 302 (temporary) hits your service every time, keeping analytics accurate. Most shorteners use 302.

Analytics: never write clicks synchronously on the redirect path. Publish an event to Kafka; consumers aggregate counts (per code, per day, per country) into a column store or Redis counters.

Follow-ups: custom aliases (unique constraint, check availability); expiry (TTL in the store + lazy check on read); abuse (rate limit creation per user/IP, scan URLs against malware lists); multi-region (replicate the read path globally, writes from one region or region-prefixed ranges).

systemdesign-ratelimiter.tldr:
• Enforce at the gateway with Redis counters updated atomically by Lua.
  • Token bucket for bursty APIs; sliding window counters for smooth limits.
  • Decide fail-open vs fail-closed when Redis is down.
  • Reduce Redis calls with local pre-limiting for very high QPS.

systemdesign-notification.tldr:
• Accept requests asynchronously (202) and fan out per channel through Kafka topics.
  • Deduplicate with idempotency keys, honour preferences and frequency caps.
  • Retry with backoff per provider, fail over between providers, dead-letter permanently failing sends.
  • Give OTPs and security alerts a priority lane.
systemdesign-notification.body:
Requirements

  • Send notifications via push (APNs/FCM), SMS, email, in-app; triggered by services (order shipped) or campaigns (marketing blast to 10M users).
  • User preferences and opt-outs; rate limits per user (no spam); templates; scheduled sends.
  • At-least-once delivery, no duplicates visible to users, delivery status tracking. Soft real-time (seconds).

Estimation: 10M transactional + up to 50M campaign notifications/day → ~600/s average, bursts of 50k/s during campaigns. Third-party providers are the bottleneck (rate-limited, slow, sometimes failing).

Send flow for one transactional notification

Data model

Key design decisions

  1. Async by default: the API validates and enqueues, returning 202 Accepted with a notification id. Callers never wait for providers.
  2. Separate topic and worker pool per channel: a slow SMS provider can't block push; scale each independently.
  3. Idempotency: callers pass a dedupKey (e.g. order-42-shipped). Store it with a TTL (Redis SET NX EX) so retries don't double-send.
  4. Preferences and quiet hours checked before enqueue; marketing respects opt-out and per-user frequency caps (Redis counters).
  5. Retries: exponential backoff via retry topics; provider-specific error handling (invalid device token → delete token, don't retry); DLQ after N attempts.
  6. Provider failover: two SMS/email providers behind an interface with a circuit breaker per provider.
  7. Campaign fan-out: a scheduler pages through the audience segment (cursor-based) and enqueues in batches with throttling, so 50M sends don't flood the system or the providers.
  8. Tracking: delivery log (Cassandra, keyed by user + time) with states QUEUED → SENT → DELIVERED/FAILED/OPENED, updated from provider webhooks.

Priority: OTPs and security alerts go to a high-priority topic with dedicated workers so a marketing campaign never delays a login code.

systemdesign-newsfeed.tldr:
• Push (fan-out on write) for normal users, pull for celebrities: the hybrid.
  • Store post ids per user in Redis, hydrate from caches, cap the list length.
  • Use cursor pagination and a separate ranking service.
  • Skip fan-out for inactive users and rebuild their feeds on login.
systemdesign-newsfeed.body:
Requirements

  • Post content; follow users; home feed shows recent posts from followed accounts, newest or ranked first, paginated.
  • Feed load < 200 ms p99; eventual consistency OK (a post may take seconds to appear); very read-heavy.

Estimation: 300M DAU, each loads feed 10×/day → 30k QPS (peak ~100k). Posts: 50M/day → ~600 writes/s. Average 200 followers; celebrities with 50M+.

Core decision: fan-out on write vs fan-out on read

Fan-out on write (push) Fan-out on read (pull)
How on post, insert post id into each follower's feed cache on feed load, query recent posts of everyone you follow and merge
Read cost O(1): read a precomputed list O(followees): expensive
Write cost O(followers): 50M writes for a celebrity O(1)
Wasted work feeds of inactive users none

Hybrid (what Twitter/Instagram do): push for normal users; for celebrities (followers above a threshold), don't fan out — merge their recent posts at read time.

Feed storage: Redis sorted set or list per user holding the latest ~800 post ids (not full posts). Hydrate ids into posts via a post cache (multi-get). Users inactive for 30 days get no fan-out; their feed is rebuilt on next login (pull).

Text
Post created by user A (5k followers):
  1. Post service stores post -> emits PostCreated
  2. Fan-out worker pages A's followers (batches of 1,000)
  3. For each active follower: ZADD feed:{follower} <timestamp> <postId>; ZREMRANGEBYRANK to cap at 800
Feed read by user B:
  1. ZREVRANGE feed:{B} offset limit  -> post ids
  2. Merge with recent posts of celebrities B follows
  3. Multi-get posts + authors from cache, filter deleted/blocked, rank, return with cursor

Pagination: cursor-based (?cursor=<lastScore>), never offset-based, because new posts keep arriving at the top.

Fan-out on write — the write path in detail

Read path — hybrid merge

Data model

Store FOLLOW twice (partitioned by follower for "whom do I follow" and by followee for "who follows me") so both fan-out and feed reads are single-partition queries.

Ranking: fetch candidates (chronological union), score with a model (engagement probability, recency, relationship strength), return top N. Keep ranking a separate service so it can evolve.

Deep dives: media goes to object storage + CDN; post deletion → tombstone and filter at read time; the social graph in a sharded store keyed by user id (both follower and following lists); hot posts (viral) cached aggressively.

systemdesign-chat.tldr:
• Clients keep WebSockets to gateways; a registry maps users to gateways.
  • Assign per-conversation sequence numbers for ordering; dedup with client message ids.
  • Store messages in Cassandra partitioned by conversation; offline users get push and sync on reconnect.
  • Publish presence only to online contacts.
systemdesign-chat.body:
Requirements

  • 1:1 and group chat (up to 500 members), online presence, delivery and read receipts, message history on multiple devices, push notifications when offline.
  • Low latency delivery (< 500 ms), messages never lost, ordered within a conversation.

Estimation: 500M DAU × 40 messages/day = 20B/day ≈ 230k messages/s. Storage: 20B × 200 B = 4 TB/day.

Connection layer: clients hold a persistent WebSocket to a chat gateway server. HTTP polling wastes resources; long polling is a fallback.

Send flow (A → B)

  1. A sends {clientMsgId, convId, text} over its socket to gateway 1.
  2. Chat service assigns a per-conversation sequence number (ordering), persists the message (Cassandra), and acks A with the server id ("sent" ✓).
  3. Looks up B's sessions in the registry. If online, routes via pub/sub to gateway 2, which pushes to B. B acks ("delivered" ✓✓).
  4. If offline, triggers a push notification; B fetches missed messages on reconnect using its last seen sequence number (GET /conversations/{id}/messages?after=seq).

Message store (Cassandra)

SQL
CREATE TABLE messages (
    conversation_id uuid,
    seq             bigint,
    message_id      uuid,
    sender_id       uuid,
    body            text,
    created_at      timestamp,
    PRIMARY KEY ((conversation_id), seq)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (seq DESC);
-- one partition per conversation; newest-first range reads for history.
-- Very large group chats: add a time bucket to the partition key to bound partition size.

Key points

  • Idempotency: clientMsgId dedups retries when the client didn't receive the ack.
  • Ordering: per-conversation sequence (Redis INCR conv:{id}:seq or a sequencer partitioned by conversation id); clients sort by seq, not by timestamps.
  • Group fan-out: for up to a few hundred members, fan out per member at send time; store the message once, deliver references.
  • Presence: gateways heartbeat; presence service keeps user → lastSeen with TTL; publish presence changes only to contacts who are online (avoid broadcast storms).
  • Gateway scaling: each gateway holds ~100k–1M connections (Netty, epoll). Use consistent hashing or a registry to find a user's gateway; on gateway crash, clients reconnect and resync from their last seq.
  • End-to-end encryption (WhatsApp/Signal protocol): server stores ciphertext only; keys exchanged per device.

systemdesign-video.tldr:
• Upload straight to object storage with pre-signed URLs; transcode asynchronously as a parallel DAG of chunks.
  • Adaptive bitrate streaming (HLS/DASH) lets the player switch renditions per segment.
  • Egress dominates cost, so the CDN hit ratio is the core of the design.
  • Count views through a stream pipeline into sharded counters, never a per-view row update.
systemdesign-video.body:
Requirements

  • Functional: upload videos; transcode into multiple resolutions; stream with adaptive quality on any device; video metadata, search, view counts.
  • Non-functional: smooth playback (start < 2 s, few rebuffers) worldwide; uploads may take minutes to process; extremely read-heavy; storage and egress cost dominate.

Estimation

Text
Uploads:        500 hours of video per minute ≈ 30k hours/hour
Raw storage:    1 hour 1080p ≈ 3 GB; ×5 renditions (240p…4K) ≈ 6-8 GB per hour of source
                -> 30k h/hour × 7 GB ≈ 210 TB per hour ≈ 5 PB/day (before dedup/cold tiering)
Views:          1B views/day, average 5 min at ~3 Mbps ≈ 110 MB per view
Egress:         1B × 110 MB ≈ 110 PB/day ≈ 10 Tbps average -> only a CDN (plus ISP caches) can serve this

The numbers say it out loud: the design is about the upload pipeline (async, parallel transcoding) and the CDN (cache hit ratio is the cost model).

Transcoding pipeline — a DAG per video

Splitting into chunks lets hundreds of workers encode one long video in parallel; a failed chunk is retried alone. Each task is idempotent (output path derived from video id + rendition + chunk index).

Adaptive bitrate streaming (HLS/DASH). The player downloads a master manifest listing renditions, then fetches 2–6 s segments, choosing the bitrate per segment from measured throughput and buffer level.

Text
#EXTM3U                                   master.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=800000,RESOLUTION=640x360
360p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=2800000,RESOLUTION=1280x720
720p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=5000000,RESOLUTION=1920x1080
1080p/index.m3u8

Data model

Deep dives

  • Upload reliability: resumable multipart upload direct to object storage with pre-signed URLs (app servers never proxy video bytes); dedup by content hash.
  • CDN strategy: popular content pushed to edges proactively (Netflix Open Connect boxes inside ISPs, filled overnight); long-tail content pulled on demand. Cache hit ratio > 95% is the goal; origin shield layer to protect storage.
  • View counts: never UPDATE videos SET views = views + 1 per view. Emit view events to Kafka, aggregate in a stream job, write sharded counters; display approximate counts.
  • Cost: keep cold renditions in infrequent-access storage; encode the long tail lazily (only 360p/720p until a video gets views); newer codecs (AV1) cut egress for popular titles.
  • Search and recommendations: metadata into Elasticsearch; recommendations from watch-history events (separate offline/online ML system).

systemdesign-filestorage.tldr:
• Split files into content-addressed blocks: delta sync uploads only changed blocks, and dedup is free.
  • A file version is an ordered list of block hashes, which makes version history cheap.
  • A per-namespace journal with a monotonic cursor lets each device ask "what changed since N?".
  • Commit with optimistic concurrency on the base version; conflicts become conflicted copies.
systemdesign-filestorage.body:
Requirements

  • Upload, download and share files; folders; automatic sync across a user's devices; version history; works offline and resolves conflicts.
  • Files up to tens of GB; sync latency of seconds; durability is non-negotiable (11 nines on the blob store).

Estimation

Text
Users:      500M total, 100M DAU, 2 devices each
Storage:    500M × 10 GB average quota used (heavy skew) ≈ 5 EB logical, much less after dedup
Changes:    100M DAU × 20 file changes/day = 2B changes/day ≈ 23k/s metadata writes

Key idea: split files into content-addressed blocks

  • Editing one slide changes one or two blocks: the client uploads only those (delta sync).
  • Identical blocks across users or versions are stored once (dedup), keyed by hash.
  • A file version is just a new list of block hashes, so version history is cheap.
  • Content-defined chunking (rolling hash boundaries) keeps blocks stable when bytes are inserted near the start.

Sync commit with optimistic concurrency

Data model

The per-namespace journal with a monotonic cursor is what makes sync simple: each device remembers its cursor and asks "what changed since 8812?".

Deep dives: sharing (shared folders are separate namespaces mounted into several users' trees; ACLs checked in the metadata service); large uploads (resumable, parallel block uploads); garbage collection (blocks with ref_count = 0 deleted after a grace period); encryption at rest per block; hot metadata shards for huge shared folders (split the namespace); bandwidth throttling and LAN sync between devices on the same network.

systemdesign-payment.tldr:
• Model payments as a persisted state machine.
  • Idempotency at every hop: client key, your id as the PSP key, idempotent webhooks.
  • On timeouts, query status instead of retrying blindly.
  • Double-entry ledger in integer minor units, outbox events, and daily reconciliation.
systemdesign-payment.body:
Requirements

  • Accept payments from customers (cards/UPI via a payment service provider like Stripe/Razorpay), credit merchants' balances, refunds, payouts to merchants, reconciliation.
  • Correctness over everything: never double-charge, never lose money, full audit trail. Availability matters, but consistency wins. Moderate scale (e.g. 1,000 TPS peak).

Payment lifecycle as a state machine: CREATED → PROCESSING → SUCCEEDED | FAILED, plus REFUND_PENDING → REFUNDED. Every transition is persisted; illegal transitions are rejected.

Idempotency end to end

  1. Client sends Idempotency-Key with the checkout request. Payment API stores key → payment order (unique constraint). Retries return the same order.
  2. Payment API passes its own payment order id as the idempotency key to the PSP, so even if we retry the PSP call after a timeout, the customer is charged once.
  3. Webhooks can arrive twice or out of order: apply transitions idempotently ("if already SUCCEEDED, ignore").

Handling the unknown outcome: a PSP call times out — did the charge happen? Never blindly retry with a new id. Mark PROCESSING, then query the PSP status API (or wait for the webhook) and reconcile.

Double-entry ledger — every money movement is two entries that sum to zero; balances are derived from entries, never updated in place without a matching entry.

SQL
CREATE TABLE ledger_entries (
    id             bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    transaction_id uuid        NOT NULL,      -- groups the debit and credit
    account_id     bigint      NOT NULL,
    amount_minor   bigint      NOT NULL,      -- paise/cents; negative = debit
    currency       char(3)     NOT NULL,
    created_at     timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
-- Customer pays 500.00 INR for an order:
--   (tx1, customer_receivable, -50000), (tx1, merchant_payable, +50000)
-- Invariant checked continuously: SUM(amount_minor) GROUP BY transaction_id = 0

Reconciliation — the safety net

Other must-mentions: store amounts as integer minor units (never floating point); append-only ledger (corrections are new entries); outbox pattern for events (payment succeeded → order service); reconciliation jobs compare internal ledger with PSP settlement reports daily and flag mismatches; PCI-DSS — never store raw card numbers (use PSP tokenization); strong consistency → relational DB with serializable or carefully locked transactions on balances.

systemdesign-flashsale.tldr:
• The challenge is absorbing millions of requests, not storing a few thousand orders.
  • Cache everything at the edge and admit users through a waiting room at a rate the backend can handle.
  • Reserve stock atomically in Redis with Lua, create orders asynchronously, and expire unpaid holds.
  • Back every fast path with a durable check: conditional updates and unique constraints in the database.
systemdesign-flashsale.body:
Requirements

  • A limited inventory (10,000 phones, or 50,000 concert seats) goes on sale at a fixed time; millions of users try to buy in the first minutes.
  • Never oversell; be fair-ish (first come first served); hold an item while the user pays (e.g. 10 minutes) and release it if unpaid; the rest of the site must stay up.

Estimation

Text
Users at 10:00:00:   5M concurrent, many refreshing → 1M+ requests/s for a few minutes
Inventory:           10,000 units → 99.8% of buyers will be told "sold out"
Successful writes:   at most 10,000 orders: the DB load is tiny IF we stop the crowd before it

The insight: the problem is not storing 10,000 orders, it's absorbing a million requests per second and converting them into 10,000 serialized decrements without melting the database.

Layered defence

  1. Static + cached everything before the sale: product page and countdown on the CDN; a "sold out" flag cached at the edge so the crowd stops hitting origin the moment stock is gone.
  2. Waiting room: users get a queue token; the system admits them at the rate the backend can handle; others see their position. This turns a spike into a steady flow.
  3. Atomic reservation in memory: a Lua script checks and decrements stock and records a hold with expiry — one round trip, no oversell, ~100k ops/s per Redis shard.
  4. Async order creation: the reservation event goes through Kafka; the order service writes durable orders at its own pace.
  5. Hold expiry: unpaid holds are released back into stock (a sorted set by expiry time, swept by a worker).
Lua
-- KEYS[1] = stock:sku1, KEYS[2] = holds:sku1 (zset: member = userId, score = expiry ms)
-- ARGV[1] = userId, ARGV[2] = now ms, ARGV[3] = hold ms, ARGV[4] = per-user limit (1)
if redis.call('ZSCORE', KEYS[2], ARGV[1]) then return -2 end          -- already holding one
local stock = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) or '0')
if stock <= 0 then return -1 end                                     -- sold out
redis.call('DECR', KEYS[1])
redis.call('ZADD', KEYS[2], tonumber(ARGV[2]) + tonumber(ARGV[3]), ARGV[1])
return stock - 1                                                     -- remaining

Seat booking variant (specific seats, BookMyShow): inventory is per seat, so contention is per row of the seats table: UPDATE show_seats SET status='HELD', held_by=?, hold_until=? WHERE show_id=? AND seat_id IN (...) AND status='AVAILABLE' and check the affected row count equals the number of seats requested (all-or-nothing in one transaction). A unique constraint on (show_id, seat_id) in the bookings table is the last line of defence.

Correctness checks to mention

Risk Guard
oversell atomic decrement (Lua / conditional UPDATE), DB unique constraints as backstop
Redis loses data on failover reconcile Redis stock against the orders DB; keep a small safety buffer; or use the DB for the final commit
one user buys everything per-user limit in the script, account + device + payment-instrument checks
bots waiting room tokens, CAPTCHA at admission, rate limits per IP/account
payment timeouts holds with expiry; idempotent payment callbacks
the rest of the shop goes down isolate the sale (separate deployment / bulkheads), shed load at the edge

systemdesign-ridehailing.tldr:
• Driver location updates (~250k/s) live in memory, not a relational DB.
  • Geo-index with geohash/H3/quadtree or Redis GEO, partitioned by city.
  • Match by ETA, offer with a timeout, and claim drivers with compare-and-set.
  • Compute surge per cell from supply and demand over a sliding window.
systemdesign-ridehailing.body:
Requirements

  • Riders request rides; nearby available drivers are matched; live driver location tracking; trip lifecycle; pricing (incl. surge); payments after the trip.
  • Matching in a few seconds; location updates every ~4 s from active drivers.

Estimation: 1M active drivers × 1 update / 4 s = 250k location writes/s — the defining load. These are ephemeral: keep them in memory, not in a relational DB.

Geo indexing — finding nearby drivers

  • Geohash: encode lat/long into a string prefix; nearby points share prefixes. Query the cell plus its 8 neighbours.
  • H3 (Uber's hexagonal grid) or S2 (Google): uniform cells at many resolutions; hexagons have equal-distance neighbours.
  • Quadtree: adaptive subdivision (dense cities get small cells).
  • Simple version: Redis GEOADD drivers:available <lng> <lat> <driverId> and GEOSEARCH ... BYRADIUS 3 km ASC COUNT 20, sharded by city.

Matching flow: rider requests → trip created (REQUESTED) → matching fetches nearest N available drivers, ranks by ETA (road distance, not straight line) → sends an offer to the best driver with a 10 s timeout → on accept, atomically mark the driver busy (compare-and-set so two trips can't grab the same driver) → trip ACCEPTED → on decline/timeout, next driver.

Driver state machine

Deep dives: partition everything by city/region (matching is local); driver state machine (offline/available/offered/on-trip) with leases; surge pricing computed per cell from demand/supply ratio over a sliding window; trip history and payments in durable SQL; location history for disputes goes to cheap storage asynchronously via Kafka.

systemdesign-scheduler.tldr:
• Claim due jobs with SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED or partitioned dispatchers.
  • Execution is at-least-once: workers heartbeat and jobs must be idempotent.
  • Recompute next_run_at for cron jobs; use timing wheels for huge timer counts.
  • Add priorities, quotas, timeouts and a catch-up policy.
systemdesign-scheduler.body:
Requirements

  • Users submit jobs to run once at a time T or on a cron schedule; jobs run on a worker fleet; retries with backoff; status and history; at-least-once execution with idempotent jobs; scale to millions of scheduled jobs.

Finding due jobs without double dispatch: partition jobs (by job_id hash) across dispatcher instances, or let dispatchers claim rows with SKIP LOCKED:

Job and execution states

SQL
-- Each dispatcher claims a batch of due jobs; concurrent dispatchers skip locked rows.
WITH due AS (
    SELECT id FROM jobs
    WHERE status = 'SCHEDULED' AND next_run_at <= now()
    ORDER BY next_run_at
    LIMIT 500
    FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
)
UPDATE jobs j SET status = 'DISPATCHED', dispatched_at = now()
FROM due WHERE j.id = due.id
RETURNING j.id, j.payload;

Execution guarantees: workers heartbeat while running; a reaper re-queues executions whose heartbeat stopped (worker crashed) → at-least-once, so job handlers must be idempotent (execution id passed to the job). Recurring jobs compute next_run_at from the cron expression after each dispatch.

Scaling to millions of timers: a DB index on (status, next_run_at) handles a lot; beyond that use time-bucketed tables or a hierarchical timing wheel in memory for the next few minutes, loaded from the DB.

Other concerns: priorities (separate queues), per-tenant quotas, job timeouts (kill and retry), catch-up policy after downtime (run missed executions once vs all), and observability (lag between scheduled and actual start time).

systemdesign-topk.tldr:
• Exact leaderboards: Redis sorted sets with O(log n) updates and ranks.
  • Trending top-K: partition by key, local heaps per partition, merge globally.
  • Count-Min Sketch bounds memory for heavy hitters at the cost of overestimates.
  • Approximate and refreshed every minute is usually good enough.
systemdesign-topk.body:
Two flavours: an exact leaderboard (game scores, contest rankings) and approximate top-K over huge streams (trending hashtags, most-viewed videos in the last hour).

Leaderboard (exact, millions of players): Redis sorted set: ZINCRBY lb:season5 <points> <userId>, ZREVRANGE lb:season5 0 99 WITHSCORES, ZREVRANK lb:season5 <userId> — all O(log n). Persist score events in a durable DB and rebuild if Redis is lost. For hundreds of millions of players, shard by score range or keep a top tier exact and approximate ranks elsewhere.

Trending top-K over a stream (billions of events/day): you can't keep an exact counter for every key in one place.

  • Partition by key so each key's count lives on one worker; each worker keeps a min-heap of its local top K; a merger combines N local top-Ks into the global top K (correct because each key lives on one partition).
  • Windows: tumbling (per minute) or sliding (last hour = sum of the last 60 one-minute buckets).
  • Count-Min Sketch when even per-partition exact counts are too big: fixed memory, over-estimates only, paired with a heap of heavy hitters.
Java
// Top-K from a frequency map with a size-K min-heap: O(n log k)
static List<String> topK(Map<String, Long> counts, int k) {
    PriorityQueue<Map.Entry<String, Long>> heap = new PriorityQueue<>(Map.Entry.comparingByValue());
    for (Map.Entry<String, Long> e : counts.entrySet()) {
        heap.offer(e);
        if (heap.size() > k) heap.poll();          // evict the smallest
    }
    List<String> result = new ArrayList<>();
    while (!heap.isEmpty()) result.add(heap.poll().getKey());
    Collections.reverse(result);
    return result;
}

Trade-off to state: exact and real-time is expensive; most products accept approximate counts and a refresh every 30–60 seconds.

systemdesign-autocomplete.tldr:
• A trie with precomputed top-K per node answers in O(prefix length).
  • Build offline from aggregated query logs and swap snapshots in.
  • Cache short prefixes at the CDN; debounce keystrokes on the client.
  • Blend in a small real-time trending layer and filter blocked terms.
systemdesign-autocomplete.body:
Requirements: as the user types, return the top 5–10 completions for the prefix within ~100 ms, ranked by popularity (and personalization); update suggestions daily or near-real-time from search logs.

Estimation: 10M DAU × 10 searches × ~6 keystrokes = 600M requests/day ≈ 7k QPS (peak 20k+). Reads dominate; data changes slowly → precompute and cache.

Data structure: a trie with cached top-K per node. Each node stores the top K completions for its prefix, so a lookup is O(prefix length), not a subtree walk.

Every node caches its top completions, so suggest("te") is three pointer hops and a list read — no subtree search at query time. The cost moves to build time and memory.

Java
class TrieNode {
    final Map<Character, TrieNode> children = new HashMap<>();
    List<String> topK = List.of();                    // precomputed, sorted by score
}

class Autocomplete {
    private final TrieNode root = new TrieNode();

    // Built offline from aggregated (query, count) pairs, then swapped in atomically
    void build(Map<String, Long> queryCounts, int k) {
        queryCounts.forEach((q, c) -> {
            TrieNode n = root;
            for (char ch : q.toCharArray()) {
                n = n.children.computeIfAbsent(ch, x -> new TrieNode());
                n.topK = merge(n.topK, q, c, k, queryCounts);
            }
        });
    }
    List<String> suggest(String prefix) {
        TrieNode n = root;
        for (char ch : prefix.toCharArray()) {
            n = n.children.get(ch);
            if (n == null) return List.of();
        }
        return n.topK;
    }
    private List<String> merge(List<String> cur, String q, long c, int k, Map<String, Long> counts) {
        List<String> next = new ArrayList<>(cur);
        if (!next.contains(q)) next.add(q);
        next.sort(Comparator.comparingLong((String s) -> counts.get(s)).reversed());
        return next.size() > k ? List.copyOf(next.subList(0, k)) : List.copyOf(next);
    }
}

Key points: shard the trie by prefix range (a–f, g–m…) or keep it fully replicated if it fits in memory; cache responses for 1–2 character prefixes at the CDN (they're few and hot); client debounces keystrokes and caches results; filter offensive or blocked terms during build; for freshness, blend a small real-time trending layer on top of the daily trie.

qa.q: How would you scale a database that's becoming a bottleneck?
qa.a: In order: optimize queries and indexes; add a cache for hot reads; add read replicas for read traffic (handle replication lag); vertical scaling; move heavy analytics to a separate store; then partition — functionally (split tables by service) and finally horizontally (shard by a key with even distribution and that most queries include). Sharding last, because it makes joins, transactions and resharding hard.

qa.q: SQL or NoSQL for this system? How do you decide?
qa.a: From access patterns and consistency needs. SQL when data is relational, needs multi-row transactions, ad-hoc queries and strong consistency (payments, orders). NoSQL (key-value/wide-column) when access is by key at very high write volume with simple queries and you can design around denormalization (messages, events, feeds, sessions). It's common to use both in one system.

qa.q: How do you choose a shard key?
qa.a: Pick a key that most queries include (so they hit one shard), with high cardinality and even distribution (no hot shards), and that keeps related data together (e.g. user_id for a user's orders). Avoid monotonically increasing keys with range sharding (all writes hit the last shard) and low-cardinality keys like country. Plan resharding with consistent hashing or many logical shards mapped onto fewer physical nodes.

qa.q: Where would you put caches, and what are the risks?
qa.a: Client/browser cache, CDN for static and media, gateway/edge cache for public GETs, application cache (Redis) for hot objects and computed results, DB buffer cache. Risks: stale data and invalidation bugs, stampedes on hot-key expiry, avalanche on mass expiry, and memory cost. Mitigate with TTLs + jitter, invalidate-on-write, request coalescing, and treating the cache as optional (system works, slower, when it's down).

qa.q: How do you make a system highly available?
qa.a: Remove single points of failure: multiple instances behind load balancers across availability zones, replicated databases with automated failover, stateless services, queues to absorb failures, timeouts/retries/circuit breakers, graceful degradation (serve cached or partial data), health checks and autoscaling, multi-region for the highest tiers, and practiced recovery (backups tested, chaos testing).

qa.q: How do you handle a celebrity or hot key problem?
qa.a: Identify it (metrics on key access). For reads: replicate the hot item to many cache nodes or a local in-process cache, CDN it. For writes (counters): shard the key into N sub-keys and aggregate on read, or batch increments. For feeds: switch from push to pull for that user. For partitions: split the hot partition or add a random suffix.

qa.q: Push vs pull for delivering updates to clients?
qa.a: Pull (polling) is simple and works through any proxy but wastes requests and adds latency. Long polling reduces waste. Server-Sent Events give server → client streaming over HTTP. WebSockets give bidirectional, low-latency streams (chat, live location) at the cost of stateful connections that need a session registry and reconnection logic. Mobile apps also rely on push notifications when the app isn't open.

qa.q: How do you guarantee a user is never charged twice?
qa.a: Idempotency keys at every hop: the client's key maps to one payment order (unique constraint); our order id is sent as the idempotency key to the PSP; webhook processing is idempotent by payment state. On timeouts we query status instead of retrying blindly, and reconciliation catches anything that slips through.

qa.q: What would you monitor in this system?
qa.a: The golden signals per service (latency percentiles, traffic, errors, saturation), business metrics (orders/min, payment success rate, notification delivery rate), queue lag, cache hit ratio, DB replication lag and connection pool usage, and SLO-based alerts (error budget burn) rather than alerting on every metric. Tracing for cross-service latency and structured logs with trace ids.

qa.q: How would you design for multiple regions?
qa.a: Decide what must be global: serve reads locally from regional replicas/caches; for writes, either single home region per entity (users pinned to a region, simpler consistency) or multi-leader with conflict resolution for data that tolerates it. Use geo-DNS/anycast for routing, replicate asynchronously, and design failover (RPO/RTO targets). Strongly consistent global data needs consensus-backed stores like Spanner/CockroachDB with higher write latency.

qa.q: Why use a message queue between services in your design?
qa.a: To decouple producers from consumers in time and availability, absorb traffic spikes (load leveling), enable fan-out to multiple consumers, retry failed processing without the caller waiting, and scale consumers independently. The cost is eventual consistency, more infrastructure and the need for idempotent consumers.

qa.q: How do you estimate the number of servers needed?
qa.a: Peak QPS ÷ sustainable QPS per server (from load tests, e.g. 1,000 req/s for a typical Spring Boot endpoint at target latency), then add headroom (~30–50%) and N+1/N+2 redundancy across zones. For example 30k peak QPS ÷ 1k = 30 servers, plus headroom → ~40–45 across three zones.

cheat.systemdesign-cheatsheet:
How to run a system design interview (45 minutes)

  • Spend 45 minutes as: requirements, estimation, API and data model, high-level design, deep dives, wrap-up.
  • Ask about users, read/write ratio, latency, consistency and must-have features first.
  • Justify every component with a requirement and state what you give up.
  • Narrate; don't jump to boxes or over-design for imaginary scale.

Back-of-the-envelope estimation cheat sheet

  • 1M requests/day ≈ 12 QPS; a day ≈ 10⁵ seconds; peaks are 2–3× (10× for events).
  • Estimate QPS, storage over years, bandwidth and cache size only where they change decisions.
  • Say assumptions out loud and draw the conclusion immediately.
  • Memorize rough capacities: Redis ~100k ops/s, a DB ~5–10k writes/s, an app server ~1–5k req/s.

Design a URL shortener (TinyURL / bit.ly)

  • Generate codes with range-allocated counters + base62 (or pre-generated keys); scramble to avoid guessable ids.
  • Redirects are the hot path: cache in Redis, 302 to keep analytics accurate.
  • Send click analytics asynchronously through Kafka.
  • Handle aliases, expiry and abuse with unique constraints, TTLs and rate limits.

Design a distributed rate limiter

  • Enforce at the gateway with Redis counters updated atomically by Lua.
  • Token bucket for bursty APIs; sliding window counters for smooth limits.
  • Decide fail-open vs fail-closed when Redis is down.
  • Reduce Redis calls with local pre-limiting for very high QPS.

Design a notification system

  • Accept requests asynchronously (202) and fan out per channel through Kafka topics.
  • Deduplicate with idempotency keys, honour preferences and frequency caps.
  • Retry with backoff per provider, fail over between providers, dead-letter permanently failing sends.
  • Give OTPs and security alerts a priority lane.

Design a news feed (Twitter / Instagram home timeline)

  • Push (fan-out on write) for normal users, pull for celebrities: the hybrid.
  • Store post ids per user in Redis, hydrate from caches, cap the list length.
  • Use cursor pagination and a separate ranking service.
  • Skip fan-out for inactive users and rebuild their feeds on login.

Design a chat system (WhatsApp / Slack)

  • Clients keep WebSockets to gateways; a registry maps users to gateways.
  • Assign per-conversation sequence numbers for ordering; dedup with client message ids.
  • Store messages in Cassandra partitioned by conversation; offline users get push and sync on reconnect.
  • Publish presence only to online contacts.

Design a video streaming platform (YouTube / Netflix)

  • Upload straight to object storage with pre-signed URLs; transcode asynchronously as a parallel DAG of chunks.
  • Adaptive bitrate streaming (HLS/DASH) lets the player switch renditions per segment.
  • Egress dominates cost, so the CDN hit ratio is the core of the design.
  • Count views through a stream pipeline into sharded counters, never a per-view row update.

Design file storage and sync (Dropbox / Google Drive)

  • Split files into content-addressed blocks: delta sync uploads only changed blocks, and dedup is free.
  • A file version is an ordered list of block hashes, which makes version history cheap.
  • A per-namespace journal with a monotonic cursor lets each device ask "what changed since N?".
  • Commit with optimistic concurrency on the base version; conflicts become conflicted copies.

Design a payment system

  • Model payments as a persisted state machine.
  • Idempotency at every hop: client key, your id as the PSP key, idempotent webhooks.
  • On timeouts, query status instead of retrying blindly.
  • Double-entry ledger in integer minor units, outbox events, and daily reconciliation.

Design a flash sale / ticket booking system (inventory under contention)

  • The challenge is absorbing millions of requests, not storing a few thousand orders.
  • Cache everything at the edge and admit users through a waiting room at a rate the backend can handle.
  • Reserve stock atomically in Redis with Lua, create orders asynchronously, and expire unpaid holds.
  • Back every fast path with a durable check: conditional updates and unique constraints in the database.

Design a ride-hailing service (Uber / Ola)

  • Driver location updates (~250k/s) live in memory, not a relational DB.
  • Geo-index with geohash/H3/quadtree or Redis GEO, partitioned by city.
  • Match by ETA, offer with a timeout, and claim drivers with compare-and-set.
  • Compute surge per cell from supply and demand over a sliding window.

Design a distributed job scheduler

  • Claim due jobs with SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED or partitioned dispatchers.
  • Execution is at-least-once: workers heartbeat and jobs must be idempotent.
  • Recompute next_run_at for cron jobs; use timing wheels for huge timer counts.
  • Add priorities, quotas, timeouts and a catch-up policy.

Design top-K / trending and a leaderboard

  • Exact leaderboards: Redis sorted sets with O(log n) updates and ranks.
  • Trending top-K: partition by key, local heaps per partition, merge globally.
  • Count-Min Sketch bounds memory for heavy hitters at the cost of overestimates.
  • Approximate and refreshed every minute is usually good enough.

Design search autocomplete (typeahead)

  • A trie with precomputed top-K per node answers in O(prefix length).
  • Build offline from aggregated query logs and swap snapshots in.
  • Cache short prefixes at the CDN; debounce keystrokes on the client.
  • Blend in a small real-time trending layer and filter blocked terms.
